A1.justification: Both PDFs describe GROOD by the same authors. Their text, equations, tables and figures support reliable comparison. v1 ends with references; v2 includes Appendix A.1-A.6. The substantial revision does not prevent matching the shared work.

before.justification: v1 reports original GROOD benchmark results, architecture comparisons, and component and interpolation ablations (Tables 1-2 and Figures 3-6).

after.justification: v2 reports original benchmark and ablation results, oracle experiments, checkpoint analyses, and additional prototype, timing and nearest-neighbor studies in the appendix.

M1.justification: v1 interpolates scored samples toward their predicted class with lambda=0.9 and constructs its OOD prototype from validation images plus uniform noise. v2 repurposes mixup toward the second-highest predicted class with lambda=0.5 to generate synthetic prototype data, removes guided interpolation from its scoring equations/algorithms, and adds proximity-based quantile filtering (Sections 4-5). The class-prototype definition also changes from correctly classified examples to all examples of each class.

E1.justification: The four core ID datasets and their near-/far-OOD test suites are retained. Auxiliary-data coverage changes through ID-derived synthetic OOD features and added CIFAR-10-C/CIFAR-100C prototype-construction evaluations (v2 Appendix A.2 and Table 6). These additions do not introduce new classification benchmarks.

E2.justification: The main comparison adds GAIA and CIDER but removes TempScale, MDSEns, Gram, OpenGAN, KLM and RankFeat (v1 Table 1 versus v2 Table 2). This substantively revises the evaluated comparator set, including adding another gradient-based competitor.

E3.justification: v2 introduces local and global oracle protocols using sampled OOD data for prototype construction and held-out OOD data for evaluation (Section 5.1.1). It also evaluates checkpoints across training, measuring stability over the last 15 epochs (Section 6.2). The main AUROC benchmark datasets and backbone configurations remain; the oracle results involve different information-access and evaluation conditions.

E4.justification: v2 adds oracle analyses, checkpoint stability, alternative prototype constructions, score-density plots, nearest-neighbor sensitivity and timing comparisons (Sections 5-6 and Appendix A.2-A.5). It removes v1's guided-interpolation ablation, perturbation-distance histogram and lambda sweeps, while revising the retained gradient/prototype component ablations.

E5.justification: Both versions retain three initialization seeds for the smaller benchmarks and one for ImageNet-1K. v2 newly reports variation across five selections of 100 OOD validation samples, with maximum AUROC standard deviation 0.5%, and standard deviations over the last 15 training epochs (Table 5). No increase in the main benchmark run counts is stated.

E6.justification: The main GROOD results are replaced under the revised method: for example, CIFAR-100 near-/far-OOD AUROC changes from 81.01/81.98 to 78.90/84.44 (v1 Table 1; v2 Table 2). Ablation and architecture results also change, and oracle, NCP-accuracy, prototype, checkpoint and timing results are added. Retained baseline entries also change, including GEN's ImageNet-200 near-OOD AUROC, 83.68 to 82.90.

T1.justification: Appendix A.6 adds a chain-rule derivation of the closed-form gradient already stated in v1. v2 Equation (5) and the derivation introduce an inconsistency by writing an OOD target, C+1, while retaining the formula for an ID-target loss; v1 Section 4.2 explicitly used an ID target. No substantial new theorem is introduced.

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution list shift from guided interpolation of scored inputs to synthetic OOD prototype generation without external OOD data, and add oracle evidence as an explicit contribution. The broader gradient/prototype detection idea remains, but the claimed distinctive mechanism and contribution scope are substantially revised.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive limitations concerning poorly clustered or noisy ID representations, gradient-storage/computation costs and prototype representativeness (Section 7). It also explains checkpoint stability, proximity filtering and the practical limits of oracle information. v1 had no comparable limitations discussion and concluded with broader applicability claims.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents FAISS/IndexIVF, identifies the first block as the synthetic-mixup location, reports runtimes, and provides a GROOD code URL described as including training/evaluation scripts. These are additional disclosures, not evidence that v1 used a different search implementation. The filtering quantile remains unspecified.

R1.justification: v2 adds rejection/SVM history and discussion of GAIA and noise-prototype methods, with new citations for CIDER, FAISS and corruption benchmarks. Some earlier background works, including Fawzi et al. on classification regions, are removed. The central positioning around neural collapse, prototypes and gradient-based OOD detection remains.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and related work are extensively rewritten, and the title is shortened. Method exposition is reordered around gradient scoring followed by prototype construction; algorithms move to Appendix A.1, and the conclusion becomes an expanded discussion with limitations. This is substantial narrative restructuring beyond the added experiments.

P2.justification: The document changes from two columns to a single-column layout. The method diagram is redrawn, t-SNE panels are redrawn and rearranged, architecture comparisons become a table, and algorithms relocate to the appendix. New oracle/checkpoint/prototype tables and diagnostic plots replace or supplement v1's displays; the interpolation plots are removed.

improvement.justification: v2 reduces v1's dependence on auxiliary OOD data and better examines prototype choice, checkpoint sensitivity and applicability limits. However, these gains coexist with new reliability problems: Equation (5)/Appendix A.6 confuse ID and OOD loss targets, and the main discussion calls GROOD best on CIFAR-100 far-OOD although Table 2 reports 84.44 versus GAIA's 86.2. These unresolved mathematical and reporting inconsistencies prevent a reliable net quality judgment.
